en: *Vajra-ābhāsa*, Scroll One.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Baodá at the Qingfa Monastery in the Capital.
A Brief Introduction to the Commentary on the *Praise of the Sūtra*, consisting of five sections. This commentary expounds upon the Imperial Commentary on the *Banzhou Sanmei Jing*.
Regarding the phrase "if one follows the classics":
"qi" (啟) means to open;
"lüe" (略) refers to the sense of being concise and essential.
The sequence of the arising of the five gates may be understood as follows:
therein, the first four provide a preliminary discussion of the meaning of the sūtra,
while the fifth provides the formal commentary on the sūtra text itself.
According to the Commentary, it is also acceptable to divide each [section] into two, resulting in ten gates.
First is the gate concerning the causes for the arising of the gradual teaching.
Regarding this, first we shall explain according to the treatise.
In the commentary (*shu*), the intent of the teaching is elucidated based on two treatises;
although their respective expositions differ,
both serve to clarify the emergence of this sutra.
It is thus because it is concise.
However, according to the commentaries of various masters, there is the sense of both the general and the specific.
The "general" refers to clarifying the overall purport of the Tathāgata’s appearance in this world and his preaching of the Dharma throughout his entire life.
This is as stated in the Lotus Sūtra:
"It is solely for the sake of one great causal matter that [the Buddha] appears in the world;
that is to say, to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision."
Because it causes [the Buddha-nature] to become pure;
because it reveals the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
because it causes one to realize the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; because it causes one to enter the path of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and so forth.
According to the *Dharmapada-śāstra*’s own commentary:
"Opening" (*kai*) signifies the supreme meaning,
because it eliminates all matters except for the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
"Showing" means having the same meaning [as the object].
"Awakening" means not knowing [the object as it appears].
"Entering" means causing one to realize the stage of non-retrogression.
It manifests immeasurable activities of wisdom.
Therefore, the commentary by Cien states:
"The All-Knowing One is the Buddha."
It is further said:
"The wise person knows it after the root.
These two are the functions of wisdom.
The nature of these two wisdoms is precisely suchness (tathatā).
Whether in terms of their function or their essence,
they are collectively designated as "wisdom."
Because the Omniscient One is called "wisdom," it is termed the "wisdom of omniscience.
Furthermore, the "Omniscient One" refers to fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
The "repeated mention of wisdom" refers to subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).
These two types of wisdom encompass the nature of wisdom, which is the wondrous principle of *tathatā* (suchness).
Furthermore, regarding "all-knowing wisdom" (*sarvajña-jñāna*):
The function of wisdom is bodhi.
The repetition of the word "wisdom" indicates that its nature is nirvāṇa;
it is now shown that both of these are entirely unsurpassed.
This simultaneously opens up both bodhi and nirvāṇa, naming them the two unsurpassed states.
Beyond these two kinds, there is nothing else;
they are called "unsurpassed" because no other thing excels these two dharmas.
The second "manifestation" specifically reveals *nirvāṇa*.
The statement that the *dharmakāya* of the three vehicles— the Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, and Buddha— is "equal and equal" is because there is no distinction between the *dharmakāya* of buddha-nature.
This means that the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) of the three vehicles is fundamentally equal.
Sentient beings, lacking wisdom, are unwilling to cultivate and realize the perfection of the dharma-body.
Thus, the Buddhas appear in the world desiring to reveal to sentient beings this nature of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
The three vehicles equally possess the equality of non-duality; because they collectively realize the fulfillment of the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya, it is called the meaning of "sameness.
As for the "three awakenings," these distinguish the various aspects of Bodhi.
Because all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not know that true state;
those who do not know the true state do not know the ultimate,
for there is only the single Buddha-vehicle.
It is because one wishes to cause sentient beings to awaken to the ultimate, singular Vehicle—
that is, the Buddha’s bodhi-wisdom— and to cultivate and grow therein that it is said they "do not know the meaning.
As for the "four entrances":
Although the preceding three [sections] have generally and specifically revealed the Buddha-fruit of bodhi and nirvāṇa, it was not yet known how these could be realized.
Now, in order to reveal the causes capable of realizing them, they are called "entrances" (praveśa).
In short, although the Buddhas appear in the world and turn the wheel of Dharma—
whether in the Great or Small Vehicles— their fundamental intent is not different.
They preach the Dharma because they desire to cause all sentient beings universally and without exception to attain Buddhahood.
Within the second, the specific intention, there are both general and specific aspects.
The general aspect clarifies the intent behind preaching the various sections of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
As stated in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*:
it is intended that one may, regarding the lack of intrinsic nature in arising and so forth,
understand as they truly are the characteristic-naturelessness (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*) and the ultimate-naturelessness (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*).
Thus, the Prajñāpāramitā is spoken of;
it is as extensively explained therein,
but fearing prolixity, I have not recorded it here.
Regarding the statement, "The Bodhisattva Asaṅga explains the intent of the three questions," it is asked:
Does one who attains the six causes and conditions explain the intent of Subhūti’s question?
Why is this used to clarify the Buddha’s intended meaning?
Answer:
As stated in the commentary, beginning from "the fundamental purport of one treatise" below.
This explains the underlying meaning.
Thus, one should know that there are six points in the intent of the question;
based on these questions, the Buddha’s responses will necessarily correspond to them.
Regarding the passage beginning with "What are those six?", all subsequent sections—
excluding the formal treatise (śāstra) itself—
demonstrate that it is the Prajñāpāramitā which ensures that the lineage of the Buddhas remains unbroken.
This summarizes the intent of the six causes.
Although there are six distinct types,
they collectively ensure that the lineage of the Buddha is never severed.
The passage beginning with "How so? is the treatise's own interrogation and explanation regarding non-interruption.
The reason for this is that the five preceding causes—starting from the severing of doubt up to the joy of benefiting sentient beings and causing their practice to progress—constitute it.
The latter [of these two] ensures that the True Teaching remains long;
through practice one will surely realize the fruit,
and when the teaching abides, the Truth remains ever luminous.
By this, the lineage of the Buddhas is able to remain uninterrupted;
however, according to this treatise,
it refers to the stages and levels (*bhūmi*).
Since the commentary itself refers to the subsequent text,
there is no need for further elaboration here.
Regarding the phrase "first, those outside the Buddha-dharma," etc.:
The sub-commentary on the section concerning the matching of stages below provides two interpretations;
this follows the intent of the former.
Thus, those prior to the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) who have not yet entered the count of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* are termed "outsiders to the Buddha-dharma."
Those who harbor doubts or fail to give rise to settled faith consist of two types of people: those who have doubts, and those who...
[are uncertain].
This is for the sake of causing those who have not yet resolved their minds to sever their doubts and enter the stage of the ten wholesome actions;
thus, this sutra is preached primarily for the purpose of severing doubt.
Those who do not yet give rise to settled faith are the bodhisattvas of the ten wholesome deeds.
This means that once doubt has been severed, faith will necessarily arise.
However, because faith is not yet fixed,
this second stage— which causes faith to arise—
causes one to enter the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) and give rise to definitive faith.
Once they have generated certain faith, they are called "insiders" of the Buddha-dharma and are counted among those who have entered the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
As for the next two categories—those who have not yet understood how to progress in their practice—they are intended to lead such people to understand and advance in their practice;
those who have entered the profound depths are led to the sixth *vihāra* (abode) and below; and those who are non-retrogressive are led to the seventh *vihāra* and above.
Both of these are termed "progressive cultivation. Regarding the latter,
for those who have already engaged in progressive cultivation but have not yet attained realization—

namely, those prior to the [first] bhūmi— it means causing them to enter the first bhūmi and beyond, wherein they personally realize the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), dwell in the abode of the Tathāgata, and attain the stage of "Great Joy" (pramuditā), which is termed "attainment through realization."
Therefore, the fifth [verse] states: "For the sake of generating joy.
Thus, although there are five causes, they are condensed into three stages.
This is because the teaching is intended only for those who have already... [and so forth].
The reason for these three stages can be understood by investigating them.
If one has already realized awakening, all verbal teachings vanish.
Question:
If entering the first stage is called "realization," does this not mean that one relies on the teachings and yet they have entirely vanished?
Answer:
This is stated according to what is predominant;
because while on the stage prior to the path of seeing, one has not yet realized the principle.
One must necessarily enter realization through faith in the teachings.
If one enters the first stage (*bhūmi*) and personally realizes *tathatā* (suchness),
one does so by relying on the contemplation of principle to realize *tathatā*.
Because the practice of contemplation based on principle is not entirely gradualist in its teaching.
The sub-commentary, in explaining the section on "entrustment," states that it mostly relies on the stage prior to the [first] bhūmi to clarify entrustment;
this is because from the first bhūmi onward, one directly realizes the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), and thus the practices for the dual benefit of self and others become powerful.
There is a verse that says:
"The Bodhisattva, abiding within the stream of Dharma,
beholds all Buddhas before and after."
"One has already drawn near to bodhi;
because there are no obstacles, it is easily attained," and so forth.
One should know that the meaning within this [passage] is likewise.
Regarding the correspondence between the arising of wisdom and the gathering of merit:
"entering the profound" refers to the arising of wisdom.
As for "gathering merit," the treatise states:
Because one who maintains and practices [this] out of desire possesses manifold merits and does not regress,
it is therefore a gathering of merit (*puṇya-saṃgraha*).
As for the assignment of these stages to specific levels, they shall be explained in the relevant passages of the text.
This is explained in the commentary on the three questions at the end of this very fascicle.

Regarding the statement that "all teachings spoken by the Buddha ultimately converge upon the two truths," although the intent of this explanation applies generally to all scriptural systems and treatises, it is here specifically applied to the present context.
However, to explain the meaning of this sūtra through such a correspondence is to use the general to interpret the particular; that is to say,
it refers to the fact that within this very [reality], nothing at all is obtained.
That which was previously described within the conventional truth—
wherein one is free from the characteristics of subject and object and does not perceive any differentiation—
is ultimately termed "non-apprehension" with respect to the ultimate principle of true nature.
Regarding these noble lineages:
all noble ones have attained them by realizing this principle of the true reality that is without marks.
"And thus one becomes a sage.
Regarding the phrase "As there is a verse that says," etc.,
this refers to a scriptural verse cited in the *Cheng weishi lun* (Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only).
The first phrase clarifies the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*);
the following three phrases clarify the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The intended meaning is as follows:
One must realize the ultimate truth in order to comprehend the conventional;
thus, all conditioned phenomena are the objects of practice for practitioners.
It is not the case that one who has not realized the ultimate truth can do so.
And it is able to realize that the conventional is like an illusion and so forth;
this establishes the meaning of the two truths explained above.
Briefly stated, there are six pairs.
Thus, there are six pairs of distinctions between the two types of knowledge: the ultimate and the conventional.
In the first pair, the knowledge that realizes the principle is the ultimate, while the knowledge of phenomenal phenomena is the conventional.
In the second pair, because it knows the true nature of all phenomena, it is called "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*).
It is called the "knowledge of all aspects" (*sarvākārajñatā*) because it knows the distinct characteristics of all phenomena;
that is, it knows them according to their various types.
Thus, the term "aspects" (*ākāra*) serves as a qualification.
The third pair is named after its metaphor:
just as a blooming lotus brings joy to all who see it,
so too does the teaching of the subsequently attained wisdom (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna) give rise to delight.
"Knowledge as-it-is" (yathāvadbhāvikajñāna) is the knowledge of suchness (tathatā).
Therefore, the Abhidharma-śāstra states: "As-it-is" means...
The three liberations, the four truths, the sixteen aspects, and so forth;
"exhausting all that exists" refers to the universal cognition of all objects within subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
Therefore, the Abhidharma-śāstra states:
"As for 'exhausting all that exists,' it refers to the exhaustion of all categories of phenomena subsumed within the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu)."
Next, regarding the general summary, there are two points:
first, to summarize the reasons for the differences between the two treatises;
second, to provide a general comparison with the sutras and the treatises.
This clarifies that the intended meanings differ in their extent,
as can be seen from the commentary.
Regarding practicing in accordance with the teachings:
By means of teaching the doctrine, one removes doubt and generates faith,
which is precisely the arousal of diligence for practice.
As for "the arising of wisdom based on the object":
The objects are the two truths.
Based upon these two truths, there arise the six pairs of wisdoms, such as the ultimate and the conventional,
as explained in the aforementioned commentary.
"Those who awaken to the profound and subtle nature of the teachings and principles" means causing them to realize the profound and wondrous principles of the Mahāyāna teachings,
which differ from the teachings of the non-Buddhists and those of the two vehicles.
Those teachings, such as those for the two vehicles, which arise from the conceptualization of the dual attachments to self and phenomena, do not avoid birth and death;
although they sever attachment to a self and attachment to phenomena,
they still persist in dwelling upon and clinging to nirvana and lack the practice of benefiting others— all such cases are not termed "profound and subtle."
Regarding the statement that "the Buddha taught the Prajñāpāramitā and so forth," according to the intent of Asaṅga’s commentary,
although it is taught, it is taught as being without teaching, thereby transcending all attachment.
The "correct" is termed non-prajñā;
therefore, the treatise states that it reveals the primary meaning (paramārtha) of the dharma-gate.
If one follows the intent of Vasubandhu’s commentary in explaining prajñā:
This is the true wisdom of all Buddhas.
"That which is not Prajñā" refers to that which is not the Prajñā attained by those of the Two Vehicles and so forth.
The intended meaning of the two treatises mentioned above both reveals the profound significance of the teaching; therefore,
this sutra was spoken in order to bring about the realization that the teaching is profound.
Within each of the meanings presented in this gateway for the arising of the teaching,
one must invariably conclude by returning to the intent of the scripture; the following sections should be understood according to this principle.
Those who have never before heard such a sutra as this—
Subhūti, having long since attained the eye of wisdom, would likewise never have heard it.
Thus, one knows that the teachings of the Mahāyāna are profound.

Regarding the statement that "the merit of upholding and explaining [the Dharma] surpasses that of giving away immeasurable bodies and wealth," this refers to the merit obtained from upholding even four lines of verse and expounding them for others;
as will be shown in the subsequent text of the sutra.
Regarding the two pairs of teachings concerning material wealth and the physical body, their measure of merit does not equal that of upholding and expounding [the Dharma].

First, within the context of the Dharmakāya characterized by merit, it is taught that the merit of bestowing the seven treasures upon a trichiliocosm is not equal to the merit of upholding and expounding even four lines of verse.

Second, regarding the abandonment of distraction toward external treatises: even the merit of giving the seven treasures as alms throughout as many trichiliocosm worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges does not equal the merit of upholding and reciting a single four-line verse.

In the third dwelling place, which is the distancing from indolence, it is taught that sacrificing as many lives as there are grains of sand in the Ganges through bodily offerings does not equal the merit of upholding and reciting even four lines of verse.

In the fourth dwelling place, which is the distancing from the savor of tranquility, it is taught that dividing a single day into three parts and sacrificing as many lives as there are grains of sand in the Ganges during each part [does not equal the merit of such practice].
To practice such immeasurable self-sacrifice for thousands of millions of billions of kalpas is not equal to hearing this sutra and having faith without opposition.
The merit obtained by one who does not oppose it— that is, one who does not slander it— is far superior.
Regarding the phrase "Thus, in the *Puṇyapradānaśāstra*, the names and so forth are determined based on the sūtras":
*Puṇyapradāna* is the title of that treatise, and *Śāstrakāra* (the author) is its name.
The title of that treatise states:
The *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra-śāstra on Destroying Attachment and Not Destroying Provisional Names*:
destroying attachment is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*);
not destroying provisional names is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Now, my view is this:
because of the two truths as established in both the sūtras and the śāstras,
it is possible to explain the titles given to the treatises and the sūtras.
Regarding the statement that this treatise explains the severing of doubt and so forth based on the stage of initial entry,
the intended meaning is as follows:
among the six causes within this treatise...
The first is for the purpose of severing doubt;
it is the very obstacle that is to be severed.
The latter four give rise to faith and so forth.
These are all included within what is cultivated.
The reason for this is explained as in the commentary (śāstra).
It should be understood that there are two kinds of obstacles: afflictions (*kleśa*).
Regarding "that which is to be known":
"obstruction" (āvaraṇa) has the sense of covering;
it is called an obstruction in the sense of hindering.
Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, fascicle nine, states:
"The afflictive hindrance refers to the view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which takes as its primary [affliction] the grasping at a real self through pervasive conceptualization."
The one hundred and twenty-eight root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*),
along with their derivative secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*),
all of which distress sentient beings' bodies and minds and obstruct *nirvāṇa*, are called the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

The cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) refers to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which takes as its primary factor the grasping at the truly existent phenomena that are conceptually imputed (*parikalpita-svabhāva*),
along with views, doubt, ignorance, attachment, aversion, pride, and so forth.
The non-erroneous nature regarding the objects of knowledge that it obscures is what obstructs bodhi;
this is called the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
When seeking its root source, the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*) are its basis.
According to the aforementioned treatise, the two views of a real self and phenomena as being conceptually constructed (*parikalpita*),
along with their associated factors— namely, false wisdom— constitute the essential nature of these two attachments.
This realm serves as the root of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*).
Question:
If that is so, are the two obstacles and the two attachments the same or different?
Answer:
Speaking of the two obstacles in general terms,
they must both take the two types of grasping as their basis;
however, when analyzed in detail:
Thus, there is a distinction between broad and narrow [scope].
Furthermore, the Master Dharmapāla explains that within the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*),
the associated view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*) is both a grasping and an obstruction.
Because it obstructs nirvāṇa;
because it involves the conception of a self-attachment;
and because it uniquely transcends greed and other afflictions without conceiving a self.
It is an obstruction but not an attachment.
Furthermore, this obstruction extends through the first seven consciousnesses,
excluding only the eighth.
The grasping [of the self] consists only of the sixth and seventh [consciousnesses], excluding the fifth and eighth.
Within the cognitive obstacles (jñeyāvaraṇa), there are likewise distinctions;
while these obstacles pervade the first seven [consciousnesses], the grasping [of the self] consists only of the sixth and seventh, and so forth.
This means that the obstruction is broad while the grasping is narrow.
According to Master Sthiramati’s commentary,
the afflictive obstruction (kleśāvaraṇa) extends through the first seven consciousnesses, excluding only the eighth.
The self-grasping (ātma-grāha) exists only in the sixth and seventh consciousnesses.
As for the cognitive obscuration (jñeya-āvaraṇa), its substance is neither broader nor narrower than that of the grasping at phenomena (dharma-grāha);
it generally pervades the first six consciousnesses as well as the eighth consciousness.
With the exception of the Buddhas,
because Bodhisattvas have not yet realized the true nature of the self-substance of the various consciousnesses,
they possess minds that pervade all three natures.
All [of these] possess attachment to phenomena (dharmagrāha),
with the sole exception of the manas;
for the treatises state that it is associated only with four [afflictions], and thus it lacks attachment to phenomena.
Furthermore, regarding the statement "there are three kinds of hindrances," these refer to the hindrances of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and maturation (*vipāka*).
They are also termed the "three defilements" (*saṃkleśa*), as commonly explained.
"The retribution is likewise inconceivable," and so forth;
this refers to the removal of the obstacle of karmic retribution.
According to the commentary by Vasubandhu, it says:
Attaining the status of Śakra, Brahmā,
and others, they immediately experience the retributive fruits of the Ten Kings and leave the three evil realms behind;
this is the removal of the obstacle of karmic retribution.
Furthermore, among the four obstacles in the *Ratnagotravibhāga*,
the first two are subsumed under the afflictive obstacle (*kleśāvaraṇa*),
while the latter two are subsumed under the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Regarding the subduing and severing [of afflictions] as explained in terms of the stage of transformative practice,
the Master of Henan states:
"The sixth mind of the ten stages of faith (daśa-śraddhā) subdues the first obstacle."
Because faith is non-retrogressive,
the fourth stage of the ten stages (daśabhūmi) subdues the second obstacle;
this is because it subdues the coarse [afflictions] of the discriminating view of self and the unshared ignorance (āveṇikāvidyā).
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"The first [type] is the noble son of the Buddha born of high lineage,
who is born from the true Dharma of the various sages and saints, and possesses all dharmas, both existent and non-existent."
Because it is free from attachment, it abandons birth and death and emerges from the triple world.
By discerning the self and that state, one can subdue these two seeds; they are severed upon entering the first stage (*bhūmi*).
The third cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is severed in the fifth stage, as it obstructs the parinirvāṇa of the lower vehicles and is therefore severed in the fifth stage.
The cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) abandoned by the mind of renunciation of the Pratyekabuddhas are severed in seven stages;
this is because they still contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination up through the sixth stage.
As for the mind of the four debts of gratitude:
This is the explanation from the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) of Liang;
it corresponds to the passage concerning the four minds— vastness and so forth—
as taught by Vasubandhu, following their respective order.
It is called "equal grace.
It is not merely the intention to bestow grace, but the true grace of benevolent intent.
The explanation of its name shall be understood in detail below.
Regarding the passage on "non-abiding nirvāṇa," according to Asaṅga’s commentary on the subsequent scriptural text,
within the "perfection of mind" there are six kinds of mind.
The fifth is named the True Mind that Does Not Dwell in Birth-and-Death.
This refers to the following passage in the sutra:
"Subhūti," [the Buddha said].

"If you should think that one who has set out for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* [should speak of] the characteristic of the annihilation and cessation of all dharmas— do not have such thoughts," and so forth;
this is because one does not abide even in *nirvāṇa*.
This universally eliminates the two obstacles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
It indicates that the six perfections encompass the precepts.
Regarding the "six equalities":
This indicates that the response fully explains the practices cultivated within the six perfections during the course of cultivation.
Furthermore, the passage beginning with "having relinquished body, wealth,
and so forth" below points to specific sections of the sūtra text and individually correlates them with the six perfections.
Furthermore, regarding "abstaining from all signs and so forth as the morality of restraint" (*saṃvara-śīla*):
among the three clusters of pure morality (*tri-koṭi-śīla*),
abstaining from all evil is called the morality of restraint.
Whatever is to be abandoned is all subsumed herein.
Now, when this sutra speaks of "generating the bodhicitta by being free from all marks," these very marks that are to be left behind are precisely the phenomena that are to be abandoned.
This is why it is called the "precept of restraining discipline.
Regarding these three clusters of pure precepts and the three types of arousal of the mind and so forth:
the first is the mind that feels weary of and seeks detachment from conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
That is to say, all phenomena associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) are the diligent abandonment of all evils.
This "diligent abandonment of all evils" is precisely the Pratimokṣa precepts.
This refers to the determination of the path, the disciplinary codes, and the precepts;
this is the morality of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*).
Second, seeking the bodhicitta consists in the universal cultivation of all virtues.
Regarding the universal cultivation of all virtues:
these consist of the true wisdom of the two kinds of emptiness,
as well as the wisdom of the emptiness of persons belonging to the two vehicles.
Even including the physical and verbal actions arising from the mundane, outflow-tainted wholesome minds of ordinary beings that accord with the Mahāyāna;
otherwise, there would be purely outflow-tainted cultivation for one kalpa prior to the stages [of the bodhisattva].
Furthermore, that which is with outflows prior to the seventh stage should not be considered "great practice";
it is precisely the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas (*śīla-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*).
Third is the mind of compassion for sentient beings.
This refers to universally observing throughout the twelve periods of day and night that the classes of sentient beings within the three realms are deeply pitiable.
"Seeking to deliver [beings] through contemplation," and so forth;
this constitutes the precept of gathering sentient beings.
In their respective order, these serve as the causes for the three types of excellence: the excellence of abandonment, the excellence of knowledge, and the excellence of benefit.
Furthermore, the two virtues of wisdom and abandonment constitute the practice for one's own benefit,
while the virtue of grace constitutes the practice for the benefit of others. These three types—
If it is prior to the stages, it is called the stage of practice through faith;
if it is on the stages, it is called the stage of the pure mind;
if it is at the level of fruition, it is called the stage of the Tathāgata.
Because all [stages] are subsumed within these three;
for the eighteen stations (*vihāra*) are condensed into the three grounds (*bhūmi*) and so forth without departing from these.
As for the treatise’s determination that they constitute the *samāpatti* (attainments) and so forth:
In the commentary on the latter part of the sutra, the Bodhisattva Asaṅga states that "one should know thus and see thus" and so forth refers to wisdom (*jñāna*).
One knows by relying upon *śamatha*,
and one sees by relying upon *vipaśyanā*.
These two are resolved through reliance on samādhi.
